title: Bun.serve(): uWebSockets C++ Engine & Zero-Copy HTTP Routing

progressiveExplaining.eli5: In Node.js, when a web request arrives, the server wraps it in many layers of JavaScript objects before your code can read it. `Bun.serve()` uses a world-record-fast C++ networking engine (`uWebSockets`) that reads and routes HTTP requests directly in native code, handling over 100,000 requests per second on a single machine.
progressiveExplaining.junior: `Bun.serve()` is Bun's built-in HTTP and WebSocket server: `Bun.serve({ port: 3000, fetch(req) { return new Response('Hello'); } })`. It uses standard Web `Request` and `Response` objects. It includes built-in static file routing, TLS/HTTPS support, Server-Sent Events (SSE), and native WebSocket handling with zero npm dependencies.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, `Bun.serve()` is built on top of a customized fork of **uWebSockets** implemented in C++ and Zig. Rather than wrapping Node's event-emitter stream abstractions, `Bun.serve` parses HTTP headers directly in native memory and lazily instantiates the JavaScriptCore `Request` object only when properties are accessed. It manages connection pooling, TLS handshakes, and TCP socket buffering directly in C++.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: `Bun.serve()` utilizes non-blocking `epoll` (Linux) or `kqueue` (macOS). When incoming TCP packets arrive, the C++ HTTP parser (picohttpparser / uWebSockets) parses the HTTP method and path in place inside the socket buffer. When returning a `Response`, Bun writes bytes directly into the socket descriptor, avoiding intermediate string copies.

codeComparison.title: Node.js http.createServer vs Bun.serve Native Server
codeComparison.summary: Node requires manual stream and socket wrapping; `Bun.serve` uses Web Standards with high-performance C++ networking.

legacyOrBad.label: Node.js http.createServer
legacyOrBad.snippet: http.createServer((req, res) => { res.writeHead(200); res.end('OK'); }).listen(3000); // ❌ Node stream API

modernOrGood.label: Bun.serve() Web Standard API
modernOrGood.snippet: Bun.serve({ port: 3000, fetch(req) { return Response.json({ status: 'healthy' }); } }); // ✅ NEW

interviewGotchas.question: How does `Bun.serve` handle WebSockets without third-party libraries like `ws` or `socket.io`?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your knowledge of Bun's native WebSocket server integration.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: `Bun.serve()` includes built-in WebSocket support using the `websocket` configuration object: `Bun.serve({ fetch(req, server) { if (server.upgrade(req)) return; return new Response('HTTP'); }, websocket: { open(ws) {}, message(ws, msg) {}, close(ws) {} } })`. The upgrade from HTTP to WebSocket happens in native C++ with zero npm dependencies.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: You do not need to install `npm install ws` in Bun; use `server.upgrade(req)` directly.

interviewGotchas.question: Can `Bun.serve` automatically serve static files directly from disk?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks knowledge of zero-copy static asset serving.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: Yes. If `fetch()` returns a `new Response(Bun.file('public/index.html'))`, Bun detects the `BunFile` and uses OS `sendfile` syscalls to pipe the file directly from disk into the TCP socket, bypassing JavaScript memory allocation.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Do not read the file into a string with `await file.text()` before returning it; returning `new Response(Bun.file(...))` directly is required for zero-copy.
